server: A computer (or computers) running 24/7 and accessible via the internet; it finds the application responsible for a request and returns the response (slide 7). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
API consumer|client: The browser or mobile app that sends requests to the web server and receives the response (slides 7, 8). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
web server: The backend machine's program that understands http requests; in this course it is written in Node.js (slide 8). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
DB server: The database server (MySQL in this course), in the same machine as the web server (local host) or in a different machine (slide 8). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
front-end: The client side of the figure: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the browser (slide 8). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
backend: The server side of the figure: web server, DB server, file server, mail server (slides 8, 10). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
server-side scripting: Code run on the server that can generate dynamic page content, work with files, collect form data and change database data (slide 9). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
dynamic page content: A page the server builds per request, as when a PHP file is run and returned in the form of html (slide 9). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
non-blocking: The server sends a task to the file system and is ready to handle the next request without waiting (slide 12). See [A server runs 24/7, and Node handles a file request in three steps](#/comp4537-l4/servers-and-server-side-scripting).
Node.js|Node, nodejs: An open-source, cross-platform, back-end JavaScript runtime environment that runs on the Chrome V8 engine and executes JavaScript outside a web browser (slide 11). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
runtime environment: The program that runs JavaScript code; Node.js is one that works outside a web browser (slide 11). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
Chrome V8|V8: The JavaScript engine Node.js runs on (slide 11). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
single-threaded|single threaded: One thread does the work, like one waiter serving every table (slides 12, 19, 20). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
asynchronous: Work is handed off and its result handled later, so the thread keeps serving others (restaurant Example 1) (slides 18, 19). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
blocking|synchronous: The thread waits for each task to finish before taking another, like the waiter waiting at the kitchen (restaurant Example 2) (slides 18, 21). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
multi-threaded: One thread per request, like one waiter dedicated to each table (restaurant Example 3) (slides 17, 18). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
thread: The unit of work the restaurant's waiter stands for; a synchronous system with 100 concurrent requests needs 100 threads (slides 22, 23). See [Node.js on V8 and the restaurant analogy](#/comp4537-l4/node-and-the-restaurant).
breakpoint: A marked line where the debugger pauses execution, such as the break point on line 2 (slides 28, 33). See [Modules with require and exports](#/comp4537-l4/node-modules).
debug console: The VS Code panel that shows console.log output while debugging (slides 26, 28). See [Modules with require and exports](#/comp4537-l4/node-modules).
module: The same as a JavaScript library; a set of functions you want to include in your application (slide 30). See [Modules with require and exports](#/comp4537-l4/node-modules).
require: Loads a module, by name for a built-in one (`require('http')`) or by path for your own (`require('./modules/math')`); the .js is optional (slides 31, 35). See [Modules with require and exports](#/comp4537-l4/node-modules).
exports: The object a module adds its functions to, as in `exports.area = function (r) {...}` (slide 31). See [Modules with require and exports](#/comp4537-l4/node-modules).
built-in module|build-in module: A module that ships with Node.js, such as http, url and fs (slides 33, 37, 40). See [Modules with require and exports](#/comp4537-l4/node-modules).
http module: Node's built-in module for creating a web server with `http.createServer` (slide 33). See [The http module: createServer, writeHead, end, listen](#/comp4537-l4/the-http-module).
createServer: `http.createServer(function (req, res) {...})` makes a server whose callback runs on each request (slides 33, 34). See [The http module: createServer, writeHead, end, listen](#/comp4537-l4/the-http-module).
writeHead: `res.writeHead(200, {...})` sends the status code and the headers such as Content-Type (slides 33, 34). See [The http module: createServer, writeHead, end, listen](#/comp4537-l4/the-http-module).
res.end|end: Finishes the response, optionally with the last text, as in `res.end('Hello World!')` (slides 33, 34). See [The http module: createServer, writeHead, end, listen](#/comp4537-l4/the-http-module).
listen: `.listen(8888)` makes the server wait for requests on port 8888 (slides 33, 34). See [The http module: createServer, writeHead, end, listen](#/comp4537-l4/the-http-module).
Content-Type: The response header naming the kind of body, such as text/html, so the browser renders the bold World! (slides 33, 34, 36). See [The http module: createServer, writeHead, end, listen](#/comp4537-l4/the-http-module).
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: The response header that tells the browser which other origins may read the response; `*` allows any (slides 34, 39). See [The http module: createServer, writeHead, end, listen](#/comp4537-l4/the-http-module).
url module: Node's built-in module used to extract the query strings in the url (slides 37, 38). See [url.parse and the query string](#/comp4537-l4/url-and-query-strings).
url.parse: `url.parse(adr, true)` splits a URL into host, pathname, search and query (slide 38). See [url.parse and the query string](#/comp4537-l4/url-and-query-strings).
query string: The part of the URL after the ?, such as ?name=John&age=23 (slides 38, 39). See [url.parse and the query string](#/comp4537-l4/url-and-query-strings).
pathname: The path part of the URL without the query, '/default.htm' (slide 38). See [url.parse and the query string](#/comp4537-l4/url-and-query-strings).
fs module|fs: The file system built-in module that allows us to work with the file system on our computer or the server (slide 40). See [The fs module and a file server that answers 404](#/comp4537-l4/fs-and-the-file-server).
readFile: `fs.readFile(filename, function (err, data) {...})` reads a file and hands its content or an error to the callback (slide 42). See [The fs module and a file server that answers 404](#/comp4537-l4/fs-and-the-file-server).
404: The status code for not found; 4xx codes mean client error (slide 42). See [The fs module and a file server that answers 404](#/comp4537-l4/fs-and-the-file-server).
phpMyAdmin: The free and open source relational DB administration tool, browser based and so working on all operating systems (slide 45). See [The fs module and a file server that answers 404](#/comp4537-l4/fs-and-the-file-server).
arrow function: The ES6 short form `(a, b) => a + b`; with one parameter the parentheses may be dropped (slide 47). See [The fs module and a file server that answers 404](#/comp4537-l4/fs-and-the-file-server).
